title: A Typewriter for the Bridge
premise: In the winter of 1914, Xanthe Fairweather drives for the formidable suffragist Lady Verity Ashcombe, reading every letter she carries and believing history belongs to other people. When the tidal causeway bridge closes for the season, a letter arrives revealing that the German engineer who once courted Verity—and to whom Verity made a deathbed-adjacent promise—has been declared an enemy alien, and his daughter is stranded on the wrong side of the war, coming to claim a legacy hidden in the Ashcombe house. As suspicion, rationing, and a zealous Home Office agent close in, Xanthe must choose between duty to her employer and the promise itself. In the end, Xanthe delivers not a letter but the truth: she forges Verity's final testament, secures the inheritance for the daughter, and discovers that belonging means being seen—by the village, by history, and by the quiet schoolmaster who has loved her all along.
about_author: Oscar Montrose is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing wartime correspondence in coastal county records offices. He writes historical fiction about the people history forgot to name.

chapters.title: The Reader of Letters
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Establishing her double life: chauffeur by day, secret reader of Lady Verity's correspondence by lamplight, convinced she is a spectator to history. She steams open a letter about the bridge closing for winter repairs. Emotional beat: comfortable invisibility, faintly hollow.

chapters.title: Lady Ashcombe's Last Campaign
chapters.summary: Verity's POV. The aging suffragist reviews her life's unfinished business: a locked writing case, a promise made in 1908 to a German engineer named Emil Brandt. She summons Xanthe with unusual gentleness. Emotional beat: mortality pressing against pride.

chapters.title: The Bridge Closes
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. The causeway shuts; the village of Marrow Quay is cut off until spring. News arrives that Britain is at war with Germany. The post slows to nothing. Emotional beat: claustrophobia disguised as coziness.

chapters.title: A Letter That Should Not Exist
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Among the last pre-closure mail, Xanthe finds a letter from Emil Brandt asking Verity to honor 'the promise' and receive his daughter Greta. Verity burns it—but Xanthe has already read it. Emotional beat: first crack in loyalty.

chapters.title: What Was Promised in Peacetime
chapters.summary: Verity's POV, 1908 flashback. Young Verity and Emil Brandt, the bridge's designer, share a season of arguments and almost-love; she promises him sanctuary at Ashcombe House should he ever need it. Emotional beat: tenderness shadowed by what duty will demand.

chapters.title: The Woman at the Gate
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Greta Brandt arrives on foot before the tide seals the road, exhausted, carrying her father's typewriter. Verity takes her in as a 'Belgian refugee'—a lie Xanthe must now maintain. Emotional beat: reluctant complicity turning to fascination.

chapters.title: The Typewriter
chapters.summary: Greta's POV. The typewriter holds letters between Emil and Verity spanning years; Greta reads them to understand why her father sent her here. Xanthe catches her, and instead of exposing her, helps hide the machine. Emotional beat: two readers becoming allies.

chapters.title: Village Eyes
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. The village gossips; the schoolmaster Thomas Penhale notices Xanthe's new secrecy and covers for her without asking why. A telegram announces a Home Office inspector will overwinter in Marrow Quay. Emotional beat: warmth entangled with dread.

chapters.title: Inspector Hale Arrives
chapters.summary: Hale's POV. The inspector, billeted at the inn, is meticulous and lonely, cataloguing aliens, deserters, and loose talk. He notes the Ashcombes' 'refugee' has no Belgian papers. Emotional beat: menace rendered polite.

chapters.title: Rationing the Truth
chapters.summary: Greta's POV. Greta works in the kitchen garden, endures slurs, and begins teaching Xanthe German words while Xanthe teaches her the village's rhythms. A near-discovery at the church jumble sale. Emotional beat: fragile belonging.

chapters.title: Verity's Collapse
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Verity suffers a stroke mid-speech at a Red Cross meeting, leaving her half-paralyzed and unable to sign anything. Suddenly the promise has no author—only witnesses. Emotional beat: panic beneath composure.

chapters.title: The Writing Case
chapters.summary: Greta's POV. Greta and Xanthe open Verity's locked writing case and find the deed naming Emil Brandt beneficiary of the cottage and annuity—unsigned, undated, worthless without execution. Emotional beat: hope curdling into impossibility.

chapters.title: Hale's Questions
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Hale interviews Xanthe about the household; her rehearsed lies begin to snag. He reveals he knows a 'Greta Brandt' was expected in Kent. Thomas intercepts a summons meant for Xanthe. Emotional beat: the net tightening.

chapters.title: Thomas's Offer
chapters.summary: Thomas's POV. The schoolmaster confesses he has loved Xanthe since she arrived and offers marriage—a paper shield of respectability for Greta and a cover story for them all. Xanthe cannot answer. Emotional beat: love offered as refuge, resented as transaction.

chapters.title: Midwinter Tide
chapters.summary: Greta's POV. On the longest night, Greta decides to leave across the frozen marshes rather than endanger the household; Xanthe stops her at the waterline, and they argue out loud for the first time about sacrifice, debt, and who owes whom. Emotional beat: fierce sisterhood forged in cold.

chapters.title: The Dictation
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Paralyzed Verity, lucid in fragments, dictates her true testament to Xanthe—naming Greta, confessing the promise, admitting Emil was the love duty cost her. She asks Xanthe to type it on Emil's machine. Emotional beat: confession as liberation.

chapters.title: Forging a Legacy
chapters.summary: Greta's POV. The legal problem: Verity cannot sign. Xanthe proposes typing the testament with Verity guiding her failing hand over the keys—an act hovering between fraud and fidelity. They do it by candlelight. Emotional beat: transgression sanctified.

chapters.title: Discovery
chapters.summary: Hale's POV. Hale finds the typed testament and matches its typeface to a typewriter reported missing from a detained German national. He comes to Ashcombe House with a constable. Emotional beat: the reckoning arriving quietly, terribly.

chapters.title: The Hearing at the Inn
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Before the village magistrate (and the whole watching village), Xanthe testifies—not denying the typing but claiming it as Verity's voice, produced before witnesses. Verity, wheeled in, presses her thumbprint to the page. Emotional beat: courage as public speech.

chapters.title: What the Village Decides
chapters.summary: Thomas's POV. The magistrate hesitates; then villagers—one by one—vouch for Greta's labor and character, shaming Hale's file into silence. Greta is registered as a ward of the parish, not an enemy. Emotional beat: community choosing mercy over fear.

chapters.title: Spring Tide
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. The bridge reopens; the first mail brings news of Emil's death in an internment camp, and Greta's grief becomes gratitude. Verity dies peacefully, her campaign finished. Xanthe delivers the last letter herself. Emotional beat: mourning braided with release.

chapters.title: A Typewriter for the Bridge
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV, epilogue. Spring 1915: Xanthe stays—not as a driver but as keeper of Verity's archive, typing the story of that winter on Emil's machine. She answers Thomas at last. History, she understands now, happened to her. Emotional beat: belonging earned, love chosen.
